raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the lifesaving benefit of defibrillation while avoiding the long-term liabilities of transvenous leads. This rationale is compelling because transvenous ICD leads are prone to fracture, insulation failure, venous obstruction, endocarditis, and difficult extraction, particularly in younger patients with decades of device exposure [1-4]. The S-ICD places the generator laterally and the electrode extrathoracically along the sternum; it senses a far-field subcutaneous electrogram and delivers high-energy shocks without intracardiac hardware [5,6].

Early feasibility work showed that ventricular fibrillation could be reliably detected and terminated with an entirely subcutaneous system [1]. The pivotal IDE study confirmed high defibrillation efficacy and acceptable short-term safety, while EFFORTLESS and pooled registry analyses demonstrated reproducible performance across broader practice, including high conversion rates for induced and spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias [6-10]. Comparative observational data suggested fewer lead-related complications than transvenous ICDs, a finding later tested in randomized trials [11]. In PRAETORIAN, the S-ICD was noninferior to the transvenous ICD for a composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks, with fewer lead-related complications but no antitachycardia pacing capability [12]. The ATLAS trial, enriched for patients at higher lead-complication risk, similarly supported a perioperative safety advantage for the S-ICD [13]. Contemporary programming and device algorithms have further improved inappropriate shock rates, as illustrated by the UNTOUCHED primary-prevention cohort [14].

Patient selection remains central. The S-ICD is best suited to patients requiring defibrillation but not chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or frequent monomorphic ventricular tachycardia likely to respond to antitachycardia pacing. It is particularly attractive in young patients, inherited arrhythmia syndromes, congenital heart disease, limited venous access, prior device infection, and dialysis or other high infection-risk states [15-23]. Conversely, patients with pacing indications, slow ventricular tachycardia, or high likelihood of future CRT generally remain better served by transvenous or extravascular systems.

Preimplant electrocardiographic screening is mandatory because the S-ICD relies on subcutaneous far-field sensing. Screening identifies patients at risk for T-wave oversensing or low R-wave amplitude, and screening failure is more common in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease, bundle-branch block, and some Brugada patterns [24]. Exercise or postural testing may be useful when repolarization changes are dynamic. Inappropriate shocks historically resulted mainly from T-wave oversensing, supraventricular tachycardia, and myopotential noise; dual-zone programming, morphology discrimination, filtering, and the SMART Pass algorithm have reduced this burden [17,18].

Implantation has evolved from a three-incision technique to a simplified two-incision approach, usually with intermuscular generator placement between the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi. This improves cosmesis, reduces pocket discomfort, and may optimize shock vector geometry [15,25]. Defibrillation testing remains debated: it verifies system integrity and shock efficacy but adds anesthesia and hemodynamic risk. Malposition is an important cause of failed conversion, and tools such as the PRAETORIAN score formalize assessment of generator and lead position [16]. Operator experience and standardized technique have reduced early complications, including hematoma, infection, and lead migration [25,26].

The main limitations of the S-ICD are intrinsic to its extravascular design. It cannot provide antibradycardia pacing, CRT, or painless antitachycardia pacing; all treated ventricular arrhythmias receive shocks. This limitation is clinically relevant for patients with recurrent monomorphic VT, although many primary-prevention patients rarely require pacing therapies. Battery longevity is shorter than some transvenous platforms because shocks are high energy, and generator size remains larger, although newer devices are smaller and longer-lived [26]. Infection is usually localized to the pocket or subcutaneous tract and generally avoids endovascular sepsis, but complete system removal is still required for established device infection [3,27].

Future directions include integration with leadless pacing, improved discrimination, smaller generators, longer battery life, remote monitoring, and modular systems capable of antitachycardia pacing without transvenous leads [28]. Current evidence supports the S-ICD as a mature alternative to the transvenous ICD for appropriately selected patients. Rather than replacing transvenous ICDs universally, it expands individualized defibrillator therapy: extravascular protection for those who need shocks, transvenous or CRT systems for those who need pacing, and shared decision-making informed by age, arrhythmia substrate, vascular access, infection risk, and patient preference [29,30].
